subject: Civil Engineering
title: The Hyatt Regency Walkway Disaster
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Hyatt Regency Walkway Disaster usable.

hook.text: In 1981, two suspended walkways collapsed during a dance. 114 people died.

buildup.text: The original design hung both walkways from the same set of long steel rods.

discovery.text: A construction change split the rods — the upper connection now carried double load.

twist.text: The change seemed minor. No engineer recalculated the new connection's capacity.

climax.text: The connection failed at the fourth-floor walkway and both decks fell in seconds.

punchline.text: A small design change ignored became a fatal mistake.

quiz.question: What caused the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse?
options: Excessive crowd weight exceeded the structural capacity
A construction change doubled the load on a connection that was never rechecked
Corrosion weakened the steel rods over many years

details.summary: On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways collapsed into the crowded lobby of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency hotel, killing 114 people and injuring 216. A seemingly minor change from continuous hanger rods to offset rods doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection.
details.whyItMatters: The Hyatt Regency collapse is structural engineering's most cited ethics case. It demonstrates how small design changes and missed checks can cause catastrophic failure, and established professional responsibility standards.
takeaways: Changing from continuous to offset hanger rods doubled the fourth-floor connection load
The original design connection was already inadequate for code-required loads
Engineers lost their licenses for failing to review the fabricator's design change

faq.question: What was the critical design change that caused the Hyatt Regency collapse?
faq.answer: The original design called for continuous threaded hanger rods passing through all walkways. The fabricator changed to offset rods, with separate rods for the upper and lower walkways.

faq.question: What professional consequences resulted from this disaster?
faq.answer: The engineers of record lost their professional engineering licenses and were barred from practicing. The case established precedents for professional responsibility, including the duty to check shop drawings and construction changes.
